originalTitle: Rising microplastics in soil a threat to UK food security, MPs and campaigners say
summary: Report calls for legally binding targets to cut microplastic pollution as soil ‘is a complex living ecosystem’
content: The accumulation of microplastics in soil presents an emerging threat to the UK’s food security, according to scientists, MPs and campaigners who have called for legally binding targets to cut microplastic pollution. UK agricultural soils have been identified as among the most contaminated by microplastics in Europe, often as a result of repeated applications of sludge from water treatment works as fertiliser, according to a report published by the all-party parliamentary group (APPG) on microplastics. With extreme weather caused by climate breakdown already placing new pressures on agriculture, protecting soil from additional and unknown pressures is becoming increasingly important, it argues. Alberto Costa, the MP for South Leicestershire and chair of the APPG, said: “Despite the evidence, the UK’s response remains limited. Existing measures tackle only a tiny proportion of microplastic emissions. We urgently need a preventative approach focused on reducing microplastic releases at source to protect human health and food security.” Prof Cressida Bowyer, the director of the Revolution Plastics Institute at the University of Portsmouth, was the senior author on the report, produced in collaboration with the APPG and the Women’s Institute. The report follows up an earlier collaboration that focused on plastic microfibres from synthetic textiles. Microplastics are pieces of plastic between 1 micrometre and 5 millimetres in size. They are often shed by the breakdown of everyday plastic items such as synthetic textiles, packaging, paints, cosmetics or car tyres. Nanoplastics are particles smaller than 1 micrometre, which makes them small enough to permeate through biological membranes. “Everywhere we look, we find them,” Bowyer said. “Doesn’t matter how deep, how high, how obscure the sampling site, we will find microplastics. And similarly we’re finding microplastics now throughout the human body.” She added: “We’re starting to realise that our exposure to microplastics is happening across the whole of the plastics lifecycle. So not just during the production phase and at the disposal end, where most people think of microplastics contamination occurring. But also during our use of plastic, when we’re using plastic packaging or when we’re wrapping ourselves in that lovely soft, cosy blanket on the sofa, or chopping our mushrooms on that plastic chopping board.” Submissions of evidence to the report showed particular concerns around the presence of microplastics in soil, which Bowyer said “impacts the biological, the chemical and the physical functioning of the soil and the soil fertility itself”. According to Bowyer, plastic particles affect the soil structure, changing the water capacity of soil; they affect the microbial community, the bacteria and fungi that are crucial to soil health; and they affect the soil fauna, with earthworms ingesting microplastics undergoing physiological changes. She said it was important to remember that “soil is not an inert material. It’s a complex living ecosystem; it’s very finely balanced. [It is a] complex ecosystem that supports the growth of crops that feed us. The second thing to remember that’s really important is that microplastics, they’re not just polymer particles … they’re basically chemical cocktails.” There are more than 16,000 chemicals used in plastics. About 4,000 are known to be harmful to health, while most of the rest have never undergone safety testing, the report notes. “Microplastics can also pick up from the environment further contaminants,” Bowyer said. “So they become like sponges or magnets for other things like bacteria, heavy metals, viral particles, other chemicals.” The report makes five policy recommendations: legally binding targets for cutting microplastic pollution, regulation of the largest sources of microplastic releases, extended producer responsibility to reduce releases across the plastics lifecycle, improved wastewater, sewage sludge and soil protections, and a coordinated national monitoring and evidence system to oversee the issue. The report’s co-author Dr Antaya March, the director of the Revolution Plastics Institute’s Global Plastics Policy Centre, said: “The UK has an opportunity to move from a fragmented response to a coordinated strategy that tackles microplastics across the plastics lifecycle. We should not wait for every scientific uncertainty to be resolved before acting where the evidence already shows that intervention can prevent pollution and reduce future risks.” The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs was contacted for comment.
chineseTitle: 议员和活动家表示，土壤中微塑料的增加对英国粮食安全构成威胁
chineseSummary: 报告呼吁制定具有法律约束力的目标，以减少微塑料污染，因为土壤“是一个复杂的生命生态系统”
chineseContent: 科学家、议员和活动人士呼吁制定具有法律约束力的目标来减少微塑料污染，他们表示，土壤中微塑料的积累对英国的粮食安全构成了新的威胁。根据跨党派议会小组（APPG）发布的关于微塑料问题的报告，英国农业土壤已被确定为欧洲受微塑料污染最严重的地区之一，这通常是由于反复使用水处理厂的污泥作为肥料造成的。报告认为，气候崩溃造成的极端天气已经给农业带来了新的压力，保护土壤免受额外和未知压力的影响变得越来越重要。南莱斯特郡议员兼 APPG 主席阿尔贝托·科斯塔 (Alberto Costa) 表示：“尽管有证据，英国的应对措施仍然有限。现有措施仅解决一小部分微塑料排放。我们迫切需要一种预防性方法，重点从源头减少微塑料排放，以保护人类健康和粮食安全。”朴茨茅斯大学革命塑料研究所所长 Cressida Bowyer 教授是该报告的资深作者，该报告是与 APPG 和妇女研究所合作编写的。该报告是早期合作的后续，该合作重点关注合成纺织品中的塑料微纤维。微塑料是尺寸在 1 微米到 5 毫米之间的塑料片。它们经常因合成纺织品、包装、油漆、化妆品或汽车轮胎等日常塑料制品的分解而脱落。纳米塑料是小于 1 微米的颗粒，这使得它们小到足以渗透生物膜。 “无论我们走到哪里，我们都能找到它们，”鲍耶说。 “无论多深、多高、多深，
